stem: A client asks what a structured product actually is at its core. Which description is correct?

options.A: A fixed-income instrument packaged together with one or more derivatives, giving a return linked to an underlying asset
options.B: A single equity security that pays a dividend linked to an index
options.C: A diversified basket of shares actively managed by a fund house
options.D: A pure derivative contract with no principal component

explanation: A structured product combines a bond or deposit (the backbone) with a derivative that delivers the market-linked payoff; it is not one single instrument. The 'single equity security' choice is wrong because a structured product is not an equity and holders do not share the issuer's profits.

stem: In the classic capital-protection build, how is the money typically allocated so the product can return principal while still offering upside?

options.A: Most of the money buys call options and a small part buys a zero-coupon bond
options.B: The money is split equally between shares and a put option
options.C: Most of the money buys a zero-coupon bond that grows back to principal, and the small remainder buys a call option for upside
options.D: All of the money buys a coupon-paying bond and the coupons buy shares

explanation: The bulk goes into a zero-coupon bond that accretes to par at maturity (returning capital), while the small leftover funds a call option for market participation. The 'most of the money buys call options' choice reverses the allocation, which would not protect capital.

stem: Since September 2009 in Singapore, what is the rule about marketing a structured product as 'capital protected'?

options.A: It may be used freely as a general marketing description
options.B: It is allowed only for structured deposits
options.C: It is required by MAS on every product summary
options.D: It is prohibited unless the product genuinely guarantees the capital

explanation: After the Lehman Minibond collapse, MAS banned the misleading 'capital protected' and 'capital guaranteed' labels from September 2009 unless the protection is genuine. The 'may be used freely' choice is exactly the misuse the rule was designed to stop.

stem: What does the 'wrapper' of a structured product determine?

options.A: The legal form, which decides how it is regulated and what protection the investor gets
options.B: The colour and design of the marketing brochure
options.C: The credit rating of the issuer
options.D: The correlation between the underlying assets

explanation: The wrapper is the legal form of delivery (deposit, note, fund, or ILP) and it drives the regulator and investor protections. The 'colour and design of the brochure' choice misses the regulatory point entirely.

stem: A customer assumes his structured deposit is covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme like his savings account. Is he correct?

options.A: Yes, all bank deposits including structured deposits are covered
options.B: No, structured deposits are excluded from the Deposit Insurance Scheme
options.C: Yes, but only up to the first year
options.D: No, but they are covered by the Policy Owners' Protection Scheme instead

explanation: A structured deposit is NOT covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme; only ordinary deposits are. The 'all bank deposits are covered' choice is the common misconception that the name 'deposit' implies the usual protection.

stem: A structured note is legally which of the following, and what does that mean if the issuer fails?

options.A: A secured bond, so the holder is repaid first from ring-fenced collateral
options.B: An equity stake, so the holder shares in any residual assets
options.C: An unsecured debenture, so the holder ranks as an unsecured creditor
options.D: A trust interest, so the assets are held separately from the issuer

explanation: A structured note is an unsecured debenture (debt) of the issuer, so on default the noteholder is merely an unsecured creditor, exactly what hurt Lehman Minibond holders. The 'secured bond' choice wrongly assumes the note is secured.

stem: Which statement about structured fund and structured ILP wrappers is correct?

options.A: A structured fund is issued only by life insurers
options.B: A structured ILP is a collective investment scheme issued by banks
options.C: Both are always issued as unsecured notes
options.D: A structured fund is a collective investment scheme, and a structured ILP is issued only by life insurers

explanation: A structured fund is a CIS, while a structured ILP is an investment-linked policy that only life insurers may issue. The 'structured fund is issued only by life insurers' choice swaps the two; only insurers issue ILPs, not funds.

stem: Structured products are commonly grouped by objective into which three types?

options.A: Capital protection, yield enhancement, and participation products
options.B: Deposits, notes, and funds
options.C: Senior, subordinated, and unsecured products
options.D: Futures, options, and swaps

explanation: By objective the three groups are capital protection, yield enhancement, and participation. The 'deposits, notes, and funds' choice lists wrappers (legal forms), not objectives.

stem: In a reverse convertible bond, what is the investor's position and its consequence?

options.A: The investor buys a put, so downside is fully hedged
options.B: The investor writes a put, earning a higher coupon but risking being delivered the shares if the price falls through the kick-in level
options.C: The investor writes a call, capping upside but with no downside risk
options.D: The investor buys a call, so the maximum loss is the premium

explanation: A reverse convertible pairs a bond with a WRITTEN put, so the investor effectively sells the put for a higher coupon and bears the downside if the underlying falls through the kick-in (typically 20-30% below start). The 'buys a put' choice reverses the option position and would not generate the enhanced yield.

stem: A discount certificate lets an investor gain exposure at a discount. What is the trade-off?

options.A: The certificate must be held to a fixed maturity with no early exit
options.B: The investor loses all dividend rights permanently
options.C: The upside is capped at a strike level in exchange for the discounted entry
options.D: The downside is unlimited in exchange for the discount

explanation: A discount certificate is built from two options: you enter at a discount but the upside is capped at a strike. The 'downside is unlimited' choice misstates the trade; the discount is bought by giving up top-end gains, not by taking unlimited downside.

stem: Among participation certificates, which correctly matches the type to its behaviour?

options.A: Tracker pays a bonus if a barrier is not breached
options.B: Airbag mirrors the underlying one-for-one
options.C: Tracker mirrors the underlying one-for-one; airbag cushions moderate falls
options.D: Bonus cushions moderate falls before losses bite

explanation: A tracker mirrors the underlying one-for-one, a bonus pays a bonus if a barrier holds, and an airbag cushions moderate falls. The 'tracker pays a bonus' choice mislabels the tracker as a bonus certificate.

stem: In a callable security, who holds the call and what risk does the investor bear?

options.A: The investor holds the call and bears no additional risk
options.B: The issuer holds a put, so the investor bears no reinvestment risk
options.C: Neither party holds an option; it is a straight bond
options.D: The issuer holds the call, so the investor bears reinvestment risk if rates fall and the issuer calls

explanation: Value equals a straight bond minus a call held by the ISSUER, so the investor is short the call and faces reinvestment risk when falling rates prompt an early call. The 'investor holds the call' choice wrongly gives the option to the investor.

stem: On issuer default, how do senior and subordinated debt rank, and what does this imply for pricing?

options.A: Subordinated ranks ahead of senior, so it should pay less
options.B: Senior ranks ahead of subordinated, so subordinated is riskier and should pay more
options.C: They rank equally, so they pay the same
options.D: Senior ranks behind subordinated, so senior should pay more

explanation: Senior debt is repaid before subordinated debt, making a subordinated note riskier and therefore it should offer a higher yield. The 'subordinated ranks ahead of senior' choice inverts the ranking.

stem: Which correctly states the SGX minimum listing thresholds for an ETF and an ETN?

options.A: ETF: at least S$750k in assets; ETN: at least S$20m in issue size
options.B: ETF: at least S$100m and 1,000 holders; ETN: at least S$5m
options.C: ETF: at least S$20m in assets and 25% held by at least 500 public holders; ETN: at least S$750k in issue size
options.D: ETF and ETN both require at least S$20m and 500 holders

explanation: An ETF needs at least S$20m in assets with 25% held by at least 500 public holders, while an ETN needs at least S$750k in issue size. The 'ETF at least S$750k / ETN at least S$20m' choice swaps the two figures.

stem: A collective investment scheme sold to retail investors in Singapore must be:

options.A: Recognised by MAS if constituted in Singapore, or authorised if overseas
options.B: Authorised by MAS if constituted in Singapore, or recognised by MAS if constituted overseas
options.C: Listed on SGX regardless of where it is constituted
options.D: Approved only by the fund manager's home regulator

explanation: A Singapore-constituted CIS is authorised by MAS; an overseas-constituted one is recognised by MAS. The 'recognised if in Singapore, authorised if overseas' choice reverses the two terms.

stem: How is the ILP sub-fund structure best described in law?

options.A: A legal trust with the policy owner as beneficiary
options.B: A partnership between the insurer and the policy owner
options.C: Not a legal trust; the insurer is legal owner in a quasi-trust arrangement
options.D: A company wholly owned by the policy owners

explanation: The ILP sub-fund is not a legal trust; the insurer is the legal owner, giving a quasi-trust arrangement governed by the Insurance Act 1966, Notice MAS 307 and the SFA 2001. The 'legal trust' choice wrongly treats it as a true trust.

stem: Under the MAS Fair Dealing Guidelines, which outcome is the key one on suitability for an adviser recommending a structured product?

options.A: Outcome 1
options.B: Outcome 4
options.C: Outcome 5
options.D: Outcome 2

explanation: Fair Dealing Outcome 2 states that products and services recommended are suitable for the customer, the central suitability standard. The other outcomes address different fair-dealing goals.

stem: Before recommending a structured product, an adviser must complete both KYC and KYP. What does KYP require?

options.A: Knowing the client's income and tax residency
options.B: Knowing the product well enough to explain it plainly to the client
options.C: Knowing the client's objectives and risk appetite
options.D: Knowing the issuer's board of directors

explanation: Know Your Product means understanding the product well enough to explain it clearly, while Know Your Client covers objectives, horizon, risk appetite and experience. The 'client's objectives and risk appetite' choice describes KYC, not KYP.

stem: The four investor objectives compete against one another. Which set correctly lists them?

options.A: Leverage, diversification, correlation, and hedging
options.B: Tax efficiency, estate planning, insurance, and liquidity
options.C: Safety of principal, income, capital growth, and liquidity
options.D: Yield, duration, convexity, and credit quality

explanation: The four competing objectives are safety of principal, income, capital growth, and liquidity, and matching a product to the client's ranked objectives is the heart of suitability. The 'leverage, diversification, correlation, hedging' choice lists risk concepts, not investor objectives.

stem: Market risk in a structured product can arise from two sources. Which pair is correct?

options.A: General market risk (broad market moves) and issuer-specific risk (events specific to the issuer or reference entity)
options.B: Liquidity risk and correlation risk
options.C: Model risk and legal risk
options.D: Currency risk and margin risk

explanation: Market risk splits into general market risk from broad moves and issuer-specific risk from events tied to the issuer or reference entity; both feed the payoff. The 'liquidity and correlation' choice lists distinct risk categories, not the two components of market risk.

stem: Why is counterparty credit risk described as central rather than peripheral to structured products, even for a 'capital protected' one?

options.A: Because the underlying shares can always fall to zero
options.B: Because MAS guarantees all structured products
options.C: Because most structured products rely on a derivative counterparty, so protection is only as good as the party providing it
options.D: Because liquidity always dries up at maturity

explanation: Most structured products depend on a derivative or swap counterparty, so any 'protection' is only as reliable as that counterparty. The 'shares can fall to zero' choice confuses market risk with counterparty risk.

stem: Which pair describes the two main defences against counterparty risk?

options.A: Diversifying the underlying and lengthening the maturity
options.B: Trading through an exchange with central clearing, or using an ISDA agreement with collateral and netting
options.C: Buying a put option and holding cash
options.D: Requiring a higher credit rating and a shorter tenor

explanation: Central clearing substitutes the clearing house as counterparty, while an ISDA agreement with collateral and netting reduces net exposure. The 'diversifying and lengthening maturity' choice addresses market risk, not counterparty risk.

stem: Liquidity risk in structured products takes two forms. Which pair is correct?

options.A: General and issuer-specific liquidity
options.B: Primary and secondary market risk
options.C: Bid liquidity and offer liquidity
options.D: Institutional liquidity risk (the market dries up) and investor liquidity risk (the investor cannot exit before maturity at a fair price)

explanation: Institutional liquidity risk is the market for the instrument drying up, while investor liquidity risk is being unable to exit before maturity at a fair price; structured products often have thin secondary markets. The 'general and issuer-specific' choice borrows the language of market risk instead.

stem: Foreign exchange risk in a structured product can arise through which two channels?

options.A: Converting principal into and out of a foreign currency, and measuring the underlying's performance in a different currency
options.B: Interest rate swaps and currency swaps only
options.C: The bid-offer spread and the front-end charge
options.D: Contango and backwardation

explanation: FX risk arises both from converting the principal in and out of a foreign currency and from measuring the underlying's return in a different currency; an adverse move can wipe out a good product return. The 'interest rate and currency swaps' choice refers to swap types, not FX exposure channels.

stem: Which of the following is an example of structural risk built into a product's design?

options.A: A broad fall in equity markets
options.B: The issuer failing to pay a coupon
options.C: A derivative trigger such as a kick-in or knock-out that changes the payoff
options.D: A shift in exchange rates

explanation: Structural risk is designed into the product, e.g. leverage, kick-in/knock-out triggers, concentration and collateral quality, and it can amplify losses beyond the underlying's move. The 'broad fall in equity markets' choice is general market risk, not structural risk.

stem: What does embedded leverage (gearing) do to a structured product's behaviour?

options.A: It dampens the effect of underlying moves on the product value
options.B: It only magnifies gains, never losses
options.C: It removes counterparty risk entirely
options.D: It makes a small move in the underlying cause a large move in the product value, cutting both ways

explanation: Gearing means a small underlying move produces a large product move, and it accelerates losses as well as gains. The 'only magnifies gains' choice is the tempting half-truth; leverage cuts both ways.

stem: How do kick-in and knock-out barrier features affect a payoff?

options.A: A kick-in guarantees a minimum return and a knock-out guarantees the maximum
options.B: A kick-in can suddenly expose the investor to losses, and a knock-out can terminate upside once a level is touched
options.C: Both simply increase the coupon with no risk
options.D: They only apply to interest rate swaps

explanation: Once a barrier level is touched, a kick-in can suddenly expose the investor to losses and a knock-out can terminate the upside; these discontinuities are a defining structural risk. The 'guarantees a minimum/maximum' choice misreads the triggers as guarantees.

stem: What lesson about legal and regulatory risk did the Lehman Minibonds episode teach?

options.A: That MAS insures all structured notes against loss
options.B: That structured notes always outperform deposits
options.C: That documentation and jurisdiction matter, as a 'safe-sounding' unsecured note referencing a defaulting entity can lead to near-total loss
options.D: That currency risk is the largest risk in structured products

explanation: The Minibonds showed how the legal structure, unsecured notes referencing a defaulting entity, turned a safe-sounding product into near-total loss, so documentation and jurisdiction matter. The 'MAS insures all structured notes' choice is false; there was no such insurance.

stem: Correlation used in multi-asset structured products ranges between which values, and why does it matter?

options.A: 0 to 1; if it shifts, only the coupon changes
options.B: -100 to +100; it only affects tax treatment
options.C: 0 to +2; it has no effect on the hedge
options.D: -1 to +1; if assumed correlations shift, the payoff and hedge behave differently than modelled

explanation: Correlation runs from -1 to +1, and multi-asset payoffs and hedges depend on assumed correlations, so a shift changes both. The '0 to 1; only the coupon changes' choice gives the wrong range and understates the impact.

stem: Modelling risk in structured products is best illustrated by which event?

options.A: The Lehman Minibond collapse
options.B: The Flash Crash, showing algorithm-driven dislocation when models break down under stress
options.C: The Asian Financial Crisis
options.D: The banning of 'capital protected' labels

explanation: Payoffs and hedges rely on models that can break down under stress; the Flash Crash is the classic illustration of algorithm-driven dislocation. The 'Lehman Minibond collapse' choice is the illustration for legal/regulatory risk, not modelling risk.

stem: Early redemption risk in a callable or auto-callable structure is a form of which broader risk?

options.A: Currency risk, since redemption is always paid in a foreign currency
options.B: Reinvestment risk, since the investor may have to reinvest in a market that has moved against them
options.C: Correlation risk, since barriers depend on multiple assets
options.D: Liquidity risk, since the secondary market always freezes

explanation: Early redemption forces the investor to reinvest, often in a market that has moved against them, so it is a form of reinvestment risk baked into callable and auto-callable structures. The 'currency risk' choice wrongly ties it to currency of payment.

stem: A derivative is best described as a contract for delayed delivery whose value derives from an underlying. Which set lists the four families?

options.A: Futures/forwards, options/warrants, swaps, and contracts for differences
options.B: Bonds, deposits, funds, and ILPs
options.C: Calls, puts, straddles, and spreads
options.D: Equities, commodities, currencies, and rates

explanation: The four derivative families are futures/forwards, options/warrants, swaps, and contracts for differences. The 'bonds, deposits, funds, ILPs' choice lists structured-product wrappers, not derivative families.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes futures from forwards?

options.A: Futures are OTC and customised; forwards are exchange-traded and standardised
options.B: Both are exchange-traded and marked to market daily
options.C: Futures are exchange-traded, standardised and margined with daily mark-to-market; forwards are OTC, customised and settled at maturity
options.D: Forwards are margined daily; futures settle only at maturity

explanation: Futures are standardised, exchange-traded, margined and marked-to-market daily, whereas forwards are customised OTC contracts settled at maturity. The 'futures are OTC / forwards are exchange-traded' choice swaps the two definitions.

stem: How is a forward price determined, and what is it NOT?

options.A: It equals spot plus cost of carry, and it is a forecast of the future spot price
options.B: It equals spot plus cost of carry (financing and storage less income), and it is an arbitrage-free relationship, not a forecast of the future spot price
options.C: It equals the average of past spot prices
options.D: It equals spot minus the risk-free rate, and it predicts the spot at expiry

explanation: Forward price equals spot plus cost of carry (financing and storage, less income); it is an arbitrage-free relationship rather than a forecast of the future spot. The choice that calls it 'a forecast of the future spot price' gets the formula right but the nature wrong.

stem: When futures trade above spot, the market is said to be in which state, and what is the basis?

options.A: Backwardation; basis is the difference between spot and futures that widens at expiry
options.B: Contango; basis is always exactly zero
options.C: Contango; basis is the difference between spot and futures that converges to zero at expiry
options.D: Backwardation; basis equals the cost of carry permanently

explanation: Futures above spot is contango (below spot is backwardation), and the basis is the spot-futures difference that converges to zero at expiry. The 'backwardation; widens at expiry' choice mislabels the state and the basis behaviour.

stem: In futures margin mechanics, what triggers a margin call and what must the trader pay?

options.A: The initial margin triggers it; the trader pays maintenance margin
options.B: Equity rising above initial margin triggers it; the trader withdraws variation margin
options.C: The exchange fee triggers it; the trader pays a commission
options.D: Equity falling to the maintenance margin triggers it; the trader tops up with variation margin

explanation: A margin call is triggered when equity falls to the maintenance margin, and the trader must post variation margin to top back up, driven by daily mark-to-market. The 'initial margin triggers it; pays maintenance margin' choice confuses the trigger with the top-up.

stem: An investor who owns a holding and wants to protect it against a price fall would use which of the following?

options.A: A short hedge, since it protects a holding you already own
options.B: A long hedge, since it protects a future purchase
options.C: A speculative long position to add exposure
options.D: A currency swap to net the cash flows

explanation: A short hedge protects a holding you already own, while a long hedge protects a future purchase; hedgers reduce existing exposure and speculators seek profit. The 'long hedge' choice applies to a future purchase, not an owned holding.

stem: To hedge an equity portfolio using index futures, how is the number of contracts (hedge ratio) determined?

options.A: By ignoring beta and matching only the dollar value
options.B: By using the correlation coefficient in place of beta
options.C: By scaling the exposure by the portfolio beta so the futures position offsets the portfolio's market sensitivity
options.D: By dividing the premium by the strike

explanation: The hedge ratio scales by the portfolio beta so the futures offset the portfolio's market sensitivity. The 'ignoring beta and matching only the dollar value' choice would under- or over-hedge a portfolio whose beta differs from 1.

stem: What is the key difference between European and American options?

options.A: European options can only be traded in Europe; American only in the US
options.B: European options are always calls; American always puts
options.C: European options have no strike price
options.D: European options exercise only at expiry; American options exercise any time up to expiry

explanation: The distinction is about timing: European options exercise only at expiry, American options any time up to expiry, regardless of geography. The 'traded only in Europe / US' choice is the common geography-based misreading.

stem: For a call option, when is it in-the-money, and how do the buyer's and writer's maximum losses compare?

options.A: In-the-money when strike > market; buyer loss unlimited, writer loss capped
options.B: In-the-money when strike < market; buyer loss capped at the premium, writer loss can be unlimited on an uncovered call
options.C: In-the-money when strike = market; both losses capped at the premium
options.D: In-the-money when strike < market; both buyer and writer risk the premium only

explanation: A call is in-the-money when the strike is below the market price; the buyer's loss is capped at the premium paid while the writer of an uncovered call faces unlimited loss. The 'strike > market; buyer loss unlimited' choice inverts both the moneyness condition and the risk profiles.

stem: Which of the following is an exotic option that pays off based on the AVERAGE price of the underlying over a period?

options.A: Barrier option
options.B: Binary (digital) option
options.C: Asian option
options.D: Lookback option

explanation: An Asian option settles on the average price of the underlying over the period. A barrier option instead depends on whether a level is touched, so that choice is a different exotic.

stem: A conservative investor holds a stock and wants income while capping upside. Which strategy fits, and how does it differ from a protective put?

options.A: Covered call (sell a call on owned stock for income); a protective put instead buys a put to insure against a fall
options.B: Protective put (sell a put on owned stock); a covered call buys a call for upside
options.C: Naked call; a protective put writes a call
options.D: Long straddle; a protective put sells both a call and a put

explanation: A covered call sells a call on stock you own to earn income while capping upside, whereas a protective put buys a put to insure against a fall. The 'protective put sells a put' choice mislabels selling a put as a protective put.

stem: What distinguishes a naked call from the offsetting-stock version, in terms of risk?

options.A: A naked call is fully covered, so risk is capped
options.B: A naked call always limits loss to the premium received
options.C: A naked call is the same as a protective put
options.D: A naked call is written without the offsetting stock, carrying open-ended risk

explanation: Writing a naked call means selling it without holding the offsetting stock, exposing the writer to open-ended risk. The 'fully covered, risk capped' choice describes a covered call, which is the opposite of naked.

stem: How do the cash flows differ between an interest rate swap and a currency swap?

options.A: Both net the cash flows and exchange no principal
options.B: An interest rate swap nets the same-currency flows; a currency swap exchanges both principal and interest in different currencies with no netting
options.C: An interest rate swap exchanges full principal; a currency swap nets the difference
options.D: Both exchange full principal and interest with no netting

explanation: In an interest rate swap the same-currency cash flows are netted so only the difference changes hands, whereas a currency swap exchanges both principal and interest in different currencies with no netting. The 'IRS exchanges full principal; currency swap nets' choice reverses the two.

stem: A distinctive feature of a credit default swap (CDS) that enables speculation is:

options.A: The protection buyer must own the reference asset
options.B: The protection seller receives the reference bond upfront
options.C: The protection buyer need NOT own the reference asset
options.D: The CDS is exchange-traded and margined daily

explanation: A CDS transfers credit risk from buyer to seller for a fee, and crucially the buyer need not own the reference asset, which allows speculation on credit. The 'buyer must own the reference asset' choice is the very requirement that CDS removes.

stem: An equity swap allows an investor to gain equity exposure by doing what?

options.A: Buying the shares outright and lending them
options.B: Purchasing a call and a put on the same strike
options.C: Netting same-currency interest cash flows only
options.D: Exchanging the equity returns for a financing leg, gaining exposure without owning the asset

explanation: An equity swap exchanges equity returns for a financing leg, and a commodity swap does the same for a commodity price, giving exposure without owning the asset outright. The 'buying the shares outright' choice defeats the purpose of a swap.

stem: For a contract for differences (CFD), which statement about dividends, financing and expiry is correct?

options.A: A CFD has a fixed expiry; long CFD pays dividends and receives interest
options.B: A CFD has no expiry and is leveraged; going long you receive dividends but pay financing interest, going short is the reverse
options.C: A CFD has no leverage; long and short both receive dividends
options.D: A CFD expires monthly; short CFD receives dividends and pays interest

explanation: A CFD is leveraged with no expiry; long positions receive dividends but pay financing interest, and short positions pay dividends but receive interest. The 'fixed expiry; long pays dividends' choice wrongly assigns an expiry and reverses the cash flows.

stem: Which description best captures what a structured ILP is?

options.A: A regular-premium participating policy with bonus smoothing
options.B: A single-premium investment-linked policy packaging term insurance with a structured investment, where the policy owner bears the full gains and losses
options.C: A capital-guaranteed deposit issued by a bank
options.D: A pure term-insurance contract with no investment element

explanation: A structured ILP is a single-premium ILP that packages term insurance with a structured investment (essentially a unit trust plus a derivative), and the policy owner takes all the investment risk. The 'participating policy with bonus smoothing' choice is wrong because there is no smoothing and it is single premium.

stem: How does a structured ILP differ from a participating (par) policy in how returns reach the owner?

options.A: The ILP smooths returns using a bonus reserve
options.B: The ILP guarantees a minimum bonus each year
options.C: The ILP has no bonus smoothing, so fund gains or losses flow straight through to the owner
options.D: The ILP pays returns only at death

explanation: Unlike a par policy, an ILP has no bonus smoothing to cushion returns, so whatever the fund earns or loses passes straight to the owner. The 'smooths returns using a bonus reserve' choice describes the par policy mechanism the ILP lacks.

stem: The death benefit of a structured ILP is best described as:

options.A: A fixed multiple of ten times the single premium
options.B: The higher of the sum assured or the cash value, which can be as low as 101% of the single premium
options.C: Always exactly equal to the single premium
options.D: The lower of sum assured or cash value

explanation: The death benefit is the higher of the sum assured or the cash value, and because the insurance element is minimal it can be as low as 101% of the single premium. The 'lower of sum assured or cash value' choice wrongly takes the lower of the two.

stem: In dual pricing, which price does the policy owner pay to buy units, and what is the typical bid-offer spread?

options.A: The bid price; spread typically 1-2%
options.B: The bid price; spread typically 3-5%
options.C: The NAV exactly; there is no spread
options.D: The offer price; spread typically 3-5%, an immediate cost on entry

explanation: The owner buys at the offer (subscription) price and sells at the bid (redemption) price, and the bid-offer spread is typically 3-5%, a cost incurred on entry. The 'bid price; 1-2%' choice confuses which price the buyer pays.

stem: Under forward pricing, at what price are ILP units dealt?

options.A: At yesterday's closing NAV, known before you transact
options.B: At the next computed NAV, so the exact price is unknown at the moment of transacting
options.C: At a fixed price set at policy inception
options.D: At the offer price plus the annual fund fee

explanation: Forward pricing means units are dealt at the next computed net asset value, so the exact price is not known when you transact. The 'yesterday's closing NAV' choice describes historic pricing, which is not how ILP units are dealt.

stem: What is the cash value or surrender value of a structured ILP equal to, and is it guaranteed?

options.A: The single premium paid, guaranteed in full
options.B: The sum assured, guaranteed at all times
options.C: The market value of the units held, with no guaranteed surrender value
options.D: The offer price of the units, fixed for the policy term

explanation: Both cash value and surrender value equal the market value of the units held, and there is no guaranteed surrender value; it floats with the fund. The 'single premium paid, guaranteed in full' choice wrongly implies a guaranteed return of premium.

stem: Which of the following is a stated advantage of a structured ILP?

options.A: Guaranteed capital return regardless of fund performance
options.B: Professional management, diversification, access to hard-to-reach instruments, and economies of scale from pooling
options.C: Zero fees in the first year
options.D: Full investor control over each trade

explanation: Advantages include professional management, diversification, access to bulky or hard-to-reach instruments, and economies of scale from pooling. The 'full investor control over each trade' choice is actually a disadvantage: the owner loses investment control.

stem: Why must a structured ILP fund earn several percent in year one just to break even?

options.A: Because MAS imposes a mandatory 5% tax
options.B: Because the death benefit consumes half the premium
options.C: Because a front-end sales charge of about 5% plus 1-2% annual fund fees create a first-year cost often around 8%
options.D: Because units are always bought above NAV by 10%

explanation: The single-premium sales charge of about 5% plus 1-2% annual fund fees push first-year total cost to roughly 8%, so the fund must earn that just to break even. The 'mandatory 5% tax' choice invents a tax that does not exist.

stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of a structured ILP?

options.A: Suitability for very short-term needs
options.B: Absence of any fees
options.C: Loss of investment control, high fees, opportunity cost of locked-up capital, and unsuitability for short horizons
options.D: Guaranteed outperformance of direct investment

explanation: Disadvantages include high fees, loss of control, opportunity cost of locked-up capital, and unsuitability for short-term needs given the long recovery horizon. The 'suitability for very short-term needs' choice states the opposite; ILPs are unsuitable for short-term needs.

stem: To protect remaining holders, ILP sub-funds are valued at least monthly and may impose which liquidity feature?

options.A: A guaranteed daily redemption at par
options.B: A lock-in of exactly five years
options.C: A redemption cap of around 10% of units, beyond which redemptions are pro-rated
options.D: A ban on all redemptions before maturity

explanation: It is common for a fund to cap single-day redemptions at around 10% of units outstanding, pro-rating requests beyond that to protect remaining holders. The 'guaranteed daily redemption at par' choice is the opposite of the liquidity constraint that actually applies.

stem: Which framework governs structured ILPs in Singapore?

options.A: Only the Companies Act
options.B: The Deposit Insurance Act only
options.C: The Financial Advisers Act 2001, the Insurance Act 1966, the Code on Collective Investment Schemes, and Notice MAS 307
options.D: The Securities and Futures Act alone, with the fund held on trust

explanation: Structured ILPs are governed by the Financial Advisers Act 2001, the Insurance Act 1966, the Code on Collective Investment Schemes, and Notice MAS 307, with the insurer as legal owner in a quasi-trust. The 'SFA alone, held on trust' choice wrongly treats the sub-fund as a trust.

stem: Under the diversification rules for an ILP sub-fund, the single-entity exposure limit is normally 10% of NAV. How does it change for an unrated corporate issue versus a government issuer?

options.A: Reduced to 5% for unrated, raised to 35% for government
options.B: Raised to 35% for unrated, reduced to 5% for government
options.C: Both raised to 20%
options.D: Both reduced to 5%

explanation: The single-entity limit is tightened to 5% for unrated or non-investment-grade debt and raised to 35% if the issuer is a government. The 'raised to 35% for unrated, reduced to 5% for government' choice reverses which issuer gets the higher ceiling.

stem: Before purchasing a structured ILP, which set of point-of-sale documents must the client receive?

options.A: Only the marketing brochure
options.B: The Product Summary, the Benefit Illustration, and the Product Highlights Sheet
options.C: Only the annual report and the audited accounts
options.D: A prospectus and a tax opinion only

explanation: The client must receive the Product Summary, the Benefit Illustration, and the Product Highlights Sheet, which disclose features, costs and risks. The 'only the marketing brochure' choice omits the mandatory disclosure documents.

stem: During the 14-day free-look period, if the policy owner cancels, what is the key caveat on the refund?

options.A: The full premium is always refunded with interest
options.B: No refund is available once the policy is issued
options.C: Only the sales charge is refunded
options.D: The refund is subject to a market value adjustment on units already invested, so the owner may not get back the full premium if units fell

explanation: Within the 14-day free-look the premium is refunded subject to a market value adjustment on any units already invested, so a fall in unit prices reduces the refund. The 'full premium always refunded with interest' choice ignores that market value adjustment.

stem: Which cadence correctly matches the after-sales reporting timelines for a structured ILP?

options.A: Statement within 30 days of the anniversary; Semi-Annual Report within 2 months; Audited Report within 3 months
options.B: Statement within 2 months; Semi-Annual Report within 3 months; Audited Report within 30 days
options.C: Statement within 3 months; Semi-Annual Report within 30 days; Audited Report within 2 months
options.D: All three within 30 days of the anniversary

explanation: The statement is due within 30 days of the policy anniversary, the Semi-Annual Report within 2 months, and the Audited Report within 3 months. The 'statement within 2 months' choice scrambles the three timelines.

stem: Which statement about the Product Highlights Sheet (PHS) rules is correct?

options.A: It may run to any length and predict actual performance
options.B: It must be at least 20 pages and show one guaranteed rate
options.C: It is capped at 4 pages of text (8 with diagrams), set in 10-point Times New Roman, carries no disclaimers, shows two hypothetical return rates, and must not predict actual performance
options.D: It may include disclaimers and a single projected return

explanation: The PHS is capped at 4 pages of text (8 with diagrams), set in 10-point Times New Roman, carries no disclaimers, must show two hypothetical rates, and the insurer shall not predict actual performance. The 'any length and predict actual performance' choice directly contradicts the no-prediction rule.

stem: Why may marketing and distribution costs NOT be charged to the ILP sub-fund?

options.A: Because MAS reimburses those costs directly
options.B: Because marketing costs are always zero for ILPs
options.C: Because the sub-fund has no NAV to charge against
options.D: Because charging them to the fund would unfairly erode existing policy owners' units

explanation: Marketing and distribution costs must not be charged to the sub-fund because doing so would unfairly erode existing policy owners' units. The 'MAS reimburses those costs' choice invents a reimbursement that does not exist.

stem: For a capital-guaranteed ILP fund, how is the payout at maturity determined?

options.A: Always the NAV, regardless of the guarantee
options.B: The higher of NAV and the guaranteed amount, with the fund valued at least monthly
options.C: The lower of NAV and the guaranteed amount
options.D: The offer price on the maturity date

explanation: For a capital-guaranteed fund the payout is the higher of NAV and the guaranteed amount, and a structured ILP must be valued at least monthly. The 'lower of NAV and the guaranteed amount' choice would defeat the guarantee.

stem: What is a portfolio bond (also called an insurance wrapper)?

options.A: A government bond bought inside a CPF account
options.B: An insurance wrapper offering a wide range of investment choices, falling within the ILP definition but giving the owner more control than a standard ILP
options.C: A fixed-coupon corporate bond with principal protection
options.D: A structured deposit sold by a bank

explanation: A portfolio bond is an insurance wrapper offering a wide range of investment choices; it falls within the ILP definition but gives the owner more control than a standard ILP. The 'fixed-coupon corporate bond' choice confuses it with an actual bond.

stem: Despite its name, why is a portfolio bond NOT a conventional bond?

options.A: Because it pays a fixed coupon linked to interest rates
options.B: Because it is guaranteed by the government
options.C: Because its value moves with the underlying investments, with no par repayment or principal protection, and any 'income' is really redemption of units
options.D: Because it always matures at par

explanation: A portfolio bond's value tracks the underlying investments rather than interest rates, there is no par repayment or principal protection, and any 'income' is really the sale (redemption) of units. The 'fixed coupon linked to interest rates' choice describes a real bond, which this is not.

stem: How does a portfolio bond give the owner more control than a standard ILP?

options.A: It lets the owner appoint managers of their portfolio within the insurer's platform and access cash, equities, bonds, derivatives and CIS
options.B: It removes all fees and guarantees the principal
options.C: It restricts the owner to a single insurer fund
options.D: It converts the ILP into a bank deposit

explanation: A standard ILP owner is limited to the insurer's funds, but a portfolio bond lets the owner appoint portfolio managers within the platform and access cash, equities, bonds, derivatives and CIS. The 'restricts to a single insurer fund' choice is the standard-ILP limitation the portfolio bond removes.

stem: What are the two headline reasons people buy portfolio bonds?

options.A: Guaranteed returns and deposit insurance
options.B: Zero fees and daily liquidity
options.C: A wide range of investment choices and tax advantages in jurisdictions where the insurance wrapper is favourably treated
options.D: Fixed coupons and principal protection

explanation: The two headline reasons are a wide range of investment choices and tax advantages where the insurance wrapper is favourably treated; they also aid succession and asset protection. The 'guaranteed returns and deposit insurance' choice wrongly implies guarantees and deposit insurance.

stem: What is 'drip-feeding' in the context of a portfolio bond?

options.A: Paying the premium in a single lump sum
options.B: Implementing a fund switch in small doses to avoid the market disruption of moving a large amount at once
options.C: Withdrawing all units on a fixed schedule
options.D: Reinvesting dividends automatically

explanation: Drip-feeding is fund-switching done in small doses, gradually moving funds to avoid the disruption of switching a large amount at once. The 'paying the premium in a single lump sum' choice describes premium payment, not fund switching.

stem: A portfolio's original 50/50 split has drifted to 63/37 through differing returns. What is rebalancing, and at what frequencies can it run automatically?

options.A: Selling everything to cash; only annually
options.B: Adding new premium to the winning asset; only once at maturity
options.C: Moving units back to restore the original risk exposure; automatically monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or annually
options.D: Locking the current 63/37 split permanently

explanation: Rebalancing moves units back to restore the original risk exposure and can run automatically monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or annually. The 'locking the current 63/37 split' choice would abandon the original allocation rather than restore it.

stem: Which of the following is one of the eight typical charges on a portfolio bond?

options.A: Deposit insurance levy
options.B: Surrender charge
options.C: Stamp duty on the premium
options.D: Central clearing fee

explanation: The eight typical charges include product charges, fund charges and transaction costs, early withdrawal charge, surrender charge, valuation charge, payment charge, dealing account debit interest, and mortality charge. The 'deposit insurance levy' choice is not among them; the stacking of these fees is a key drawback.

stem: Why is a portfolio bond marketed as a 'lifestyle' policy?

options.A: Because it pays out on lifestyle events like weddings
options.B: Because one adjustable policy matches changing objectives over a lifetime: capital appreciation in the 30s-40s, safety near retirement, then income stability plus safety afterwards
options.C: Because it is only sold to high-net-worth clients
options.D: Because it guarantees a fixed lifestyle income

explanation: It is a 'lifestyle' policy because one adjustable policy can match shifting objectives over a lifetime, from capital appreciation in the 30s-40s to safety near retirement and income stability plus safety afterwards. The 'pays out on lifestyle events' choice misreads 'lifestyle' as an event-linked payout.

stem: The consolidation advantage of a portfolio bond comes at what cost?

options.A: Loss of all investment choice
options.B: No statement is provided at all
options.C: High charges, because insurers invest heavily in systems to integrate managers' reporting into a single consolidated statement
options.D: Mandatory annual switching

explanation: A single consolidated statement replaces many fund-manager statements, but this convenience comes with high charges since insurers invest heavily in the integrating systems. The 'loss of all investment choice' choice misstates the trade-off; choice is not lost, cost is the price.

stem: For which client is a portfolio bond LEAST suitable?

options.A: A client wanting mainly insurance protection, or with only a 3 to 5-year horizon, or who does not need the flexibility
options.B: A high-net-worth client seeking wide investment choice over the long term
options.C: A client wanting to appoint their own portfolio managers
options.D: A client seeking succession and asset-protection planning

explanation: Portfolio bonds are unsuitable for those seeking insurance protection (death cover is minimal), those with a 3 to 5-year horizon (fees need a long runway), and those who do not need the flexibility. Remember the tax benefit can be outweighed by the cost, and tax laws can change. The 'high-net-worth client seeking wide choice' describes an ideal candidate, not an unsuitable one.

stem: What is the recommended lens for reading a structured ILP case study?

options.A: Memorise the payout table only
options.B: Work through product features, selling points, risk analysis, and performance under different market scenarios
options.C: Focus solely on the guaranteed rate
options.D: Compare only the fees against a bank deposit

explanation: Chapter 6 tests application, so each case should be read through the same lens: product features, selling points, risk analysis, and performance under different market scenarios. The 'memorise the payout table only' choice reduces application to rote recall.

stem: In the Superior Income Plan (SIP), the annual payout is the HIGHER of which two amounts?

options.A: A guaranteed 20% of single premium, or a non-guaranteed 4% x n/N
options.B: A guaranteed 4% of single premium, or a non-guaranteed 20% x n/N, where n is trading days all six stocks are at or above 92% and N is total trading days
options.C: A guaranteed 8% of single premium, or a non-guaranteed 108% x n/N
options.D: A fixed 4% regardless of stock performance

explanation: The SIP pays the higher of a guaranteed 4% of single premium or a non-guaranteed 20% x n/N, where n counts trading days all six stocks are at or above 92% of their start and N is total trading days. The 'guaranteed 20% / non-guaranteed 4%' choice swaps the two figures.

stem: In the SIP, what role do the six reference stocks play?

options.A: They are the actual holdings the single premium is invested in
options.B: They are only a benchmark to set the payout and trigger early redemption; the actual assets are the ILP sub-fund holdings
options.C: They are the guarantor of the 4% minimum
options.D: They determine the death benefit multiple

explanation: The single premium is NOT invested in the six stocks; they are only a reference benchmark to determine the payout and early redemption, while the real assets are the ILP sub-fund holdings. The 'actual holdings' choice is the exact misconception the case warns against.

stem: Why does the WORST-performing of the six stocks effectively govern the SIP's non-guaranteed payout?

options.A: Because the payout averages the six stock returns
options.B: Because only the best stock is measured
options.C: Because a day counts only when ALL six stocks are at or above 92%, so a single stock dipping below 92% makes that day count for nothing
options.D: Because the guarantor picks the worst stock deliberately

explanation: n counts only days when all six stocks are at or above 92%, so one stock below 92% on a day zeroes that day, meaning the worst performer governs the outcome and six stocks make beating 4% far less likely. The 'averages the six stock returns' choice wrongly assumes averaging.

stem: In the SIP, what does the 108% figure represent, and what is the maximum return under the policy?

options.A: It is the maximum return of 8% per year
options.B: It is an early-redemption trigger; the maximum return is 20% p.a., not 8%
options.C: It is the guaranteed minimum payout
options.D: It is the death benefit as a percentage of premium

explanation: The 108% is an early-redemption trigger (ABC can redeem after the third month if all six stocks are at or above 108%), and the maximum return is 20% p.a., never 8%. The 'maximum return of 8%' choice is exactly the confusion the case tells you to avoid.

stem: Why is the best stock performance NOT the best result for the SIP policy owner?

options.A: Because strong performance breaches the guarantee
options.B: Because the death benefit falls when stocks rise
options.C: Because the return is capped at 20% p.a. and strong performance triggers early redemption, forcing reinvestment and losing further upside
options.D: Because the guarantor cancels the policy on a rally

explanation: With the return capped at 20% p.a. and no downside (barring surrender or guarantor failure), the strongest stock performance triggers early redemption, causing reinvestment risk plus lost upside. The 'breaches the guarantee' choice misstates the mechanism; the guarantee is not breached.

stem: In the SIP, who provides the guarantee of the 4% minimum and principal, and where does the counterparty risk sit?

options.A: ABC the insurer provides it, so risk sits with ABC
options.B: MAS provides it, so there is no counterparty risk
options.C: The six reference stocks jointly provide it
options.D: XYZ Bank, a non-related third party, provides it and the guarantee ends if XYZ is liquidated, so the counterparty risk sits with XYZ

explanation: The guarantee is provided by XYZ Bank, a non-related entity, and the policy states it ends if XYZ goes into liquidation, so the counterparty risk sits with XYZ rather than ABC. Without that clause ABC as primary party would have to honour it, so the wording shifts the risk to the investor.

stem: In the SIP, a 5% initial fee is deducted from NAV on day one plus a 1.5% annual fund management fee. What is the immediate consequence?

options.A: The fund must earn at least 5% just to break even
options.B: The fund is guaranteed to break even in year one
options.C: The 1.5% fee is refunded at maturity
options.D: The initial fee is added to the death benefit

explanation: Because the 5% initial fee is deducted from NAV upfront, the fund must earn at least 5% just to break even, a direct market-risk consequence of the fee load. The 'guaranteed to break even' choice ignores that the upfront fee creates a hurdle, not a guarantee.

stem: Across the four SIP scenarios, which is actually the BEST outcome for the policy owner?

options.A: Best-case market performance (all six reach 108% in 3 months), which triggers early redemption
options.B: Moderate performance (all six stay between 92% and 108%), giving the full 20%/yr for a S$20,000 total on S$10,000
options.C: Worst-case performance (all six below 92%), giving the guaranteed 4%/yr
options.D: Mixed performance (at least one below 92% on any day)

explanation: Moderate performance keeps n = N so the full 20%/yr applies, totalling S$20,000 on a S$10,000 premium over five years, the best outcome. The 'best market performance' label is a trap: it triggers early redemption and only one 4.8% payout of S$480.

stem: In Case 2 (Lifestyle Plan), what type of policy is it and what is the death/TPD benefit?

options.A: A single-premium term policy paying 101% of premium on death
options.B: A par whole-life policy with smoothed bonuses
options.C: A recurrent-single-premium whole-life ILP investing in the structured 'Choice Fund', with a guaranteed death or TPD benefit of 125% of premiums paid; surrender pays 100% of NAV
options.D: A structured deposit paying 125% at maturity

explanation: The Lifestyle Plan is a recurrent-single-premium whole-life ILP investing in the structured Choice Fund, a closed-ended fund with a fixed maturity; death or TPD benefit is a guaranteed 125% of premiums paid and surrender pays 100% of NAV. The 'single-premium term policy paying 101%' choice understates the death benefit and mislabels the policy.

stem: In the Choice Fund, what exactly is the Secure Price?

options.A: A guaranteed minimum maturity value
options.B: The offer price at inception
options.C: A target the manager strives for, set yearly at the insurer's discretion; if per-unit NAV is below it at maturity, the payout is the unit price, not the Secure Price
options.D: A floor enforced by MAS

explanation: The Secure Price is an aspiration, not a floor: it is a yearly target set at the insurer's discretion, and if NAV is below it at maturity the payout is the unit price. The 'guaranteed minimum maturity value' choice wrongly treats it as a guarantee; this is a non-guaranteed product.

stem: Which risk is specifically raised for the Choice Fund given its S$6.8m size and heavy OTC fixed-income holdings?

options.A: Currency risk from overseas listing
options.B: Liquidity risk, as the small fund heavily invested in OTC fixed income may not meet high withdrawal demand
options.C: Deposit insurance risk
options.D: Inflation-indexation risk

explanation: The Choice Fund's small S$6.8m size and heavy OTC fixed-income holdings create liquidity risk, so it may temporarily be unable to meet high withdrawal demand. Other cited risks are non-guarantee, market risk (NAV down about 7%), and derivatives risk from the external Golden Derivative Fund.

stem: Why is it hard for a client to assess the Choice Fund's inherent market risk?

options.A: Because the fund publishes no NAV
options.B: Because the fund is denominated in a foreign currency
options.C: Because the fund has no fixed asset allocation and no performance benchmark, so the manager may shift the asset mix sharply
options.D: Because the fund is capital guaranteed

explanation: With no fixed asset allocation and no performance benchmark, the manager can shift the asset mix sharply, making the inherent market risk hard to assess. The 'publishes no NAV' choice is false; the case reports a NAV of S$0.9293.

stem: In Case 2, a 1% switching fee is applied to a S$10,000 investment. How much is available to invest after the fee?

options.A: S$10,000, since the fee is waived
options.B: S$9,900, after a S$100 switching fee
options.C: S$9,000, after a S$1,000 switching fee
options.D: S$9,950, after a S$50 switching fee

explanation: A 1% switching fee on S$10,000 is S$100, leaving S$9,900 to invest. The 'S$9,000 after a S$1,000 fee' choice applies 10% instead of 1%; the front-end sales charge here is 5% on each recurrent premium plus a 1-2% annual fund fee.

stem: When judging a fund against its benchmark, why must the assessment period be stated?

options.A: Because the benchmark changes daily
options.B: Because a fund can outperform over one horizon and underperform over another, so the period must be specified
options.C: Because benchmarks are only valid for one year
options.D: Because performance is guaranteed over five years

explanation: A fund can beat the benchmark over one horizon yet lag over another, so the period must be stated when judging performance. For example, a fund may outperform the index over three years but underperform over one year.

stem: SIP, Scenario 1 (Best): An investor pays a S$10,000 single premium. All six stocks gradually rise to 108% three months after inception, none falling below 92% in that period. There are 60 qualifying trading days out of an annual 250. Using the higher of guaranteed 4% or 20% x n/N, prorated for three months, what single payout does the investor receive at early redemption?
explanation: Non-guaranteed = 20% x 60/250 = 4.8%, which exceeds the guaranteed 4%, so the rate is 4.8%. Payout = S$10,000 x 4.8% = S$480, paid once at early redemption after three months. The S$400 option wrongly applies the lower guaranteed 4% instead of the higher 4.8%.

stem: SIP, Scenario 2 (Worst): On a S$10,000 single premium, all six stocks stay consistently below 92% for the full 5 years, so n = 0 every year. Counting all five annual payouts plus the return of the single premium at maturity, what is the total the policy owner receives over the 5 years?
explanation: With n = 0 the non-guaranteed 20% x n/N is 0, so the guaranteed 4% applies: 4% x S$10,000 = S$400 per year x 5 years = S$2,000, plus the S$10,000 premium returned at maturity = S$12,000. The S$2,000 option counts only the payouts and forgets the returned premium.

stem: SIP, Scenario 3 (Moderate): On a S$10,000 single premium, all six stocks trade consistently between 92% and 108% for all 5 years, so n = N every year. Including all five annual payouts and the return of the single premium at maturity, what is the total received?
explanation: Since n = N, the non-guaranteed 20% x n/N = 20%, higher than the guaranteed 4%, so each year pays 20% x S$10,000 = S$2,000. Over 5 years that is S$10,000, plus the S$10,000 premium returned = S$20,000. The S$12,000 option applies the guaranteed 4% instead of the higher 20%.

stem: A SIP invests a S$10,000 single premium. A 5% initial fee is deducted from NAV on day one, and a 1.5% annual fund management fee is charged. Immediately after the initial fee, what is the invested NAV, and roughly what percentage must the fund earn on that post-fee amount to recover back to S$10,000?

options.A: NAV S$9,500; must earn about 5.26% to get back to S$10,000
options.B: NAV S$9,500; must earn exactly 5% to get back to S$10,000
options.C: NAV S$5,000; must earn 100% to get back to S$10,000
options.D: NAV S$9,850; must earn about 1.5% to get back to S$10,000

explanation: The 5% initial fee on S$10,000 is S$500, leaving S$9,500 invested. To climb from S$9,500 back to S$10,000 the fund must gain S$500, i.e. 500/9,500 = 5.26%. The 'exactly 5%' option is the common error of assuming a 5% loss is recovered by a 5% gain, but recovering a fall always needs a slightly larger percentage gain.

stem: In the Lifestyle Plan (Case 2), a policy owner wants to switch S$10,000 between sub-funds. The switching fee is 1%. After paying the switching fee, the amount invested then falls by a further 5% front-end sales charge applicable on the new allocation. How much is actually put to work in the new sub-fund?
explanation: The 1% switching fee on S$10,000 is S$100, leaving S$9,900. Applying the 5% front-end charge: S$9,900 x 5% = S$495, so S$9,900 - S$495 = S$9,405 is invested. The S$9,900 option stops after the switching fee and ignores the 5% front-end charge.

stem: A structured ILP charges a 5% single-premium sales charge on entry plus a 2% annual fund management fee, giving a first-year total cost of about 7% of a S$20,000 premium. In dollar terms, roughly how much must the fund generate in year one just to break even?

options.A: About S$400
options.B: About S$1,400
options.C: About S$2,000
options.D: About S$140

explanation: First-year cost is about 7% of S$20,000 = S$1,400 (5% sales charge = S$1,000 plus 2% fund fee = S$400), so the fund must earn roughly S$1,400 just to break even. The 'about S$400' option counts only the 2% fund fee and ignores the 5% sales charge.

stem: An adviser tells a client that a structured product is 'basically a share that pays interest'. Which description should the adviser have given instead?

options.A: A pre-packaged investment combining a fixed-income instrument with one or more derivatives, so the return is linked to an underlying asset
options.B: A single exchange-traded derivative with no bond component
options.C: A diversified portfolio of listed shares managed passively
options.D: An ordinary bank deposit paying a fixed interest rate

explanation: A structured product is not a single instrument: it packages a bond or deposit (the backbone) with one or more derivatives (the market-linked payoff). The 'single exchange-traded derivative' description misses the fixed-income component entirely, and a fixed-rate deposit has no market-linked derivative at all.

stem: In 2010 a client shows you a Singapore product brochure describing a note as 'capital protected'. What should this tell you?

options.A: Something is wrong: from September 2009 issuers in Singapore may not use 'capital protected' or 'capital guaranteed' unless the product genuinely is
options.B: The label is fine as long as a risk disclaimer is attached
options.C: The term has been banned in Singapore since 2001
options.D: The label is permitted for any note approved for SGX listing

explanation: The use of 'capital / principal protected' and derivatives of the term has been disallowed in Singapore from September 2009, after the Lehman Minibond episode showed how the label misled investors. Attaching a disclaimer does not make the banned term permissible, and the ban dates from September 2009, not 2001.

stem: Two structured products have identical payoff formulas, but one is issued as a note and the other as a fund. What difference does the wrapper make?

options.A: It changes the underlying asset the payoff references
options.B: It determines how the product is regulated and what protection the investor gets
options.C: It has no effect; only the payoff formula matters
options.D: It fixes the product's credit rating

explanation: The wrapper is the legal form of delivery (structured deposit, note, fund or ILP), and it decides the regulatory regime and investor protections that apply. Two identical payoffs can leave investors in very different legal positions, so 'no effect' is wrong, and the wrapper neither changes the referenced underlying nor sets a credit rating.

stem: A retiree moves money from a fixed deposit into a structured deposit at the same bank, believing the same safety net applies. What has changed?

options.A: Nothing; both are covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme
options.B: The structured deposit is treated as an investment product and is excluded from the Deposit Insurance Scheme
options.C: The structured deposit gains extra protection because it is an investment product
options.D: The structured deposit is covered only up to half the normal insured limit

explanation: Structured deposits are considered investment products and are excluded from the Deposit Insurance Scheme in Singapore, unlike the ordinary fixed deposit the retiree left. There is no partial or enhanced coverage; the exclusion is total.

stem: An investor buys a structured note. Legally, what is the investor's position relative to the issuer?

options.A: A lender holding an unsecured debenture, ranking as an unsecured creditor if the issuer fails
options.B: A secured creditor with a claim over the underlying assets
options.C: A shareholder of the issuer
options.D: A depositor protected by the Deposit Insurance Scheme

explanation: A structured note is an unsecured debenture: the note-holder is lending money to the issuer and stands as an unsecured creditor on default, which is exactly what hurt Lehman Minibond holders. The investor holds no security over underlying assets, owns no shares, and has no deposit insurance cover.

stem: Which pairing of wrapper and issuer is correct?

options.A: Structured ILP issued only by a life insurer, operating like term insurance plus a structured fund
options.B: Structured ILP issued by any licensed bank
options.C: Structured fund issued as an unsecured debenture of the manager
options.D: Structured deposit issued by a fund management company

explanation: Only life insurers can issue structured ILPs, which operate like a term insurance policy combined with a structured fund. Banks cannot issue ILPs, a structured fund is a collective investment scheme rather than a debenture, and only banks can take deposits, so a fund manager cannot issue a structured deposit.

stem: A client wants exposure that mirrors an index's performance rather than protecting capital or boosting coupon income. By objective, which product category fits?

options.A: A participation product
options.B: A capital protection product
options.C: A yield enhancement product
options.D: A guaranteed income product

explanation: Structured products are grouped by objective into capital protection, yield enhancement, and participation products, and one that aims to mirror the underlying belongs to the participation family. Capital protection prioritises principal, yield enhancement trades upside for coupon, and 'guaranteed income product' is not one of the three categories.

stem: Among participation certificates, which type cushions moderate falls in the underlying before losses start to bite?

options.A: An airbag certificate
options.B: A tracker certificate
options.C: A bonus certificate
options.D: A discount certificate

explanation: The airbag certificate is the participation product designed to cushion moderate declines before losses begin. A tracker simply mirrors the underlying one-for-one, a bonus certificate pays a bonus if a barrier is not breached, and a discount certificate is a yield enhancement product, not a participation certificate.

stem: Interest rates have fallen sharply since a callable structured note was issued. What is the issuer most likely to do, and what does that mean for the investor?

options.A: Call the note to refinance at the lower rate, leaving the investor to reinvest at lower yields
options.B: Let the note run, since falling rates make calling unattractive
options.C: Call the note, which benefits the investor because rates are lower
options.D: Nothing, because the investor holds the call option

explanation: The issuer holds the call and will exercise it when rates decline so it can refinance its debt more cheaply, which forces the investor to reinvest at lower rates. The investor is short the call, not long it, and being repaid early in a low-rate environment is a cost to the investor, not a benefit.

stem: An issuer offers two structured notes identical except that one is senior and the other subordinated. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The subordinated note ranks behind the senior note on default and should offer a higher return
options.B: The subordinated note ranks ahead of the senior note on default
options.C: Both rank equally; the labels affect only maturity
options.D: The senior note should pay more because it ranks first

explanation: On issuer default, senior debt is repaid ahead of subordinated debt, so the subordinated note carries more risk and should compensate with a higher return. Ranking is about repayment priority, not maturity, and the safer senior note should pay less, not more.

stem: To list an ETF on SGX, apart from the minimum S$20 million fund size, what public spread is required?

options.A: At least 25% of issued shares held by at least 500 public shareholders
options.B: At least 50% of issued shares held by at least 100 public shareholders
options.C: At least 10% of issued shares held by at least 500 public shareholders
options.D: At least 80% of the issue subscribed by specified investors

explanation: SGX requires an ETF to have at least S$20 million in fund size with at least 25% of issued shares (excluding treasury shares) held by at least 500 public shareholders (100 in the case of a venture capital fund). The '80% subscribed by specified investors' condition applies to certain ETN issuers whose equities are not listed on SGX, not to ETFs.

stem: A fund manager wants to sell a collective investment scheme constituted in Luxembourg to Singapore retail investors. What MAS status must the scheme have?

options.A: Recognised by MAS, because it is constituted overseas
options.B: Authorised by MAS, because all retail schemes are authorised
options.C: No MAS status; SGX approval suffices
options.D: Exempted by MAS as a foreign scheme

explanation: A CIS offered to retail investors must be authorised by MAS if constituted in Singapore, or recognised by MAS if constituted overseas, so a Luxembourg-constituted scheme needs recognition. Authorisation is reserved for Singapore-constituted schemes, and SGX approval is not a substitute for MAS status.

stem: Who is the legal owner of the assets in an ILP sub-fund, and what is the arrangement called?

options.A: The insurer is the legal owner, in a quasi-trust arrangement rather than a legal trust
options.B: An independent trustee is the legal owner under a formal trust deed
options.C: Each policy owner is the legal owner of a pro-rata share of the assets
options.D: MAS holds the assets on behalf of policy owners

explanation: An ILP sub-fund is not a legal trust; the insurer is the legal owner of the assets, giving a quasi-trust arrangement governed by the Insurance Act 1966, Notice MAS 307 and the Securities and Futures Act 2001. There is no independent trustee holding legal title, policy owners hold units rather than the assets, and MAS is the regulator, not a custodian.

stem: When were the MAS Fair Dealing Guidelines issued, and how many desired outcomes do they set out?

options.A: April 2009, with five desired outcomes
options.B: September 2009, with two desired outcomes
options.C: April 2009, with ten desired outcomes
options.D: April 2001, with five desired outcomes

explanation: The MAS Guidelines on Fair Dealing were issued in April 2009 and outline five desired outcomes, with Outcome 2 requiring that products and services recommended are suitable for the customer. September 2009 is the date the 'capital protected' label was banned, a separate development.

stem: An adviser has thoroughly documented a client's objectives, horizon and risk appetite, but cannot explain in plain terms how the recommended note's barrier feature works. What requirement is not met?

options.A: Know Your Product: the adviser must understand the product well enough to explain it plainly
options.B: Know Your Client: the fact-find is incomplete
options.C: None; documenting the client profile is sufficient
options.D: The free-look requirement

explanation: Both Know Your Client and Know Your Product are required before recommending a structured product, and an adviser who cannot plainly explain the barrier feature fails Know Your Product even with a complete client profile. The fact-find here is done, so Know Your Client is satisfied, and the free-look is a post-sale cancellation right, not an advisory duty.

stem: A client wants maximum safety of principal, high income, strong capital growth and instant liquidity all at once. What should the adviser explain?

options.A: The four objectives compete: gaining more of one usually means giving up another, so the client must rank them
options.B: A structured product can deliver all four objectives simultaneously
options.C: Safety and liquidity are the same objective, so only three need considering
options.D: Income and capital growth always move together

explanation: Safety of principal, income, capital growth and liquidity are the four investor objectives, and they trade off against each other, so suitability starts with ranking them. No product delivers all four at once, safety and liquidity are distinct objectives, and income and growth typically pull in different directions rather than moving together.

stem: A 5-year S$100 note puts S$80 into a zero-coupon bond maturing at S$100 par, and S$20 into a call option on ABC shares with a strike of S$120 (current price S$100). At maturity ABC trades at S$150. What does the note pay?
explanation: The zero-coupon bond matures at S$100, and the call pays S$150 - S$120 = S$30, so the note pays S$100 + S$30 = S$130. The S$150 figure is what a direct shareholding would be worth, ignoring the note structure; S$100 is the payout only if the option expires worthless (share at or below S$120).

stem: An investor holds a S$10,000 reverse convertible note paying an 8% coupon, linked to a stock issued at S$10 with a kick-in level 25% below issue (S$7.50). The predetermined delivery is 1,000 shares in lieu of par. At maturity the stock is at S$7.00, below the kick-in level. Counting the coupon, what is the total value the investor receives?
explanation: The kick-in level is breached, so instead of the S$10,000 par the investor receives 1,000 shares worth 1,000 x S$7.00 = S$7,000, plus the coupon of 8% x S$10,000 = S$800, giving S$7,800. The S$10,800 figure assumes par is still repaid despite the breach, and S$7,000 forgets the coupon, which is still paid.

stem: An investor buys a discount certificate for S$90 on a stock trading at S$100, with a cap-strike of S$110. At maturity the stock trades at S$120, above the cap. What is the investor's profit per certificate?
explanation: Above the cap-strike the investor receives a cash settlement equal to the cap-strike of S$110, the maximum possible, so profit = S$110 - S$90 = S$20. The S$30 figure wrongly assumes uncapped participation up to the S$120 share price; the cap is exactly what the entry discount compensates for.

stem: A structured note's underlying stock falls 15% during a broad market sell-off in which the whole index drops. Which risk has materialised?

options.A: General market risk, since the fall came from a broad market move rather than an issuer-specific event
options.B: Issuer-specific risk, since only this stock matters to the note
options.C: Liquidity risk, since prices fell
options.D: Modelling risk, since the payoff formula was affected

explanation: A decline driven by a broad market move is general market risk; issuer-specific risk arises from events particular to the issuer or reference entity, such as a profit warning at that company alone. Falling prices are not in themselves liquidity risk, and no model failure is described.

stem: A client says a product marketed with a full capital guarantee 'cannot lose money'. What risk remains even if the guarantee is genuine?

options.A: Counterparty risk: the guarantee is only as good as the party providing it
options.B: No risk at all; a guarantee removes every risk
options.C: Only inflation risk, which is not a real risk
options.D: Correlation risk between the guarantor and the client

explanation: Even a genuinely guaranteed product carries counterparty credit risk, because the issuer or guarantor may fail to pay; protection is only as good as the party standing behind it. Claiming a guarantee removes every risk is precisely the misconception, and correlation risk concerns multi-asset payoffs, not this situation.

stem: A dealer wants to reduce counterparty risk on an over-the-counter derivative that cannot be moved onto an exchange. Which mechanism helps most directly?

options.A: An ISDA agreement with collateral and netting to reduce the net exposure
options.B: Buying more of the same derivative from the same counterparty
options.C: Extending the maturity of the contract
options.D: Removing the margin requirement

explanation: The two main defences against counterparty risk are central clearing through an exchange (the clearing house substitutes as counterparty) and, for OTC trades, an ISDA agreement with collateral and netting to shrink net exposure. Concentrating more exposure with the same counterparty or stretching the maturity increases risk, and removing margin removes protection.

stem: An investor holding a 5-year structured note needs cash in year 2 but finds she can only sell at a heavy discount because there is almost no secondary market. Which risk is this?

options.A: Investor liquidity risk: she cannot exit before maturity at a fair price
options.B: Credit risk of the issuer
options.C: Foreign exchange risk
options.D: Early redemption risk triggered by the issuer

explanation: Being unable to exit before maturity at a fair price is investor liquidity risk, one of the two forms of liquidity risk alongside institutional liquidity risk (the market for the instrument drying up). The issuer has not defaulted, no currency is involved, and it is the investor seeking exit, not the issuer calling the note.

stem: A Singapore investor buys a structured product whose underlying is measured in US dollars. The underlying gains 10%, but the US dollar weakens sharply against the Singapore dollar. What can happen to her return?

options.A: The good underlying return can be wiped out by the adverse currency move
options.B: Nothing; currency moves never affect structured products
